---

## I. The Colour That Changed Civilisation

Of all the colours that have shaped human history, none has wielded such raw, enduring power as purple. It has toppled fortunes, defined empires, encoded divinity, and even entered the language — to "don the purple" once meant to become emperor. Its story spans Bronze Age beaches, the laboratories of Victorian chemists, and the wardrobes of modern royalty. It is a story of rarity, ambition, and transformation.

---

answer_text:
# Purple: A History of the World's Most Royal Colour

---

## I. The Colour That Changed Civilisation

Of all the colours that have shaped human history, none has wielded such raw, enduring power as purple. It has toppled fortunes, defined empires, encoded divinity, and even entered the language — to "don the purple" once meant to become emperor. Its story spans Bronze Age beaches, the laboratories of Victorian chemists, and the wardrobes of modern royalty. It is a story of rarity, ambition, and transformation.

---

## II. The Myth of Its Birth

Every great colour deserves a creation myth, and purple has one worthy of its grandeur. In Phoenician mythology, the discovery of purple was credited to the pet dog of Tyros, the mistress of Tyre's patron god Melqart. One day, while walking along the beach, the couple noticed that after biting on a washed-up mollusc, the dog's mouth was stained purple. Tyros asked for a garment made of the same colour — and so began the famous dyeing industry. A separate Greek legend attributes the discovery to Hercules himself, who made the same observation after his dog chewed on a sea snail. However it was discovered, the discovery was seismic.

---

## III. The Phoenicians: Purple as Power and Profit

Tyrian purple — also known as Royal purple or Imperial purple — is a dye extracted from the murex shellfish, first produced by the Phoenician city of Tyre in the Bronze Age. Its difficulty of manufacture, striking purple-to-red colour range, and resistance to fading made clothing dyed with it highly desirable and expensive.

The name "Phoenician" may even have meant "purple people," from an ancient Greek word for the colour of the mythical phoenix. And the mysterious purple dye may have been one reason for the Phoenicians' success. The Phoenicians were traders from the eastern Mediterranean whose city-states rose after about 1200 BC, when many neighbouring Bronze Age powers collapsed. The biblical cities of Tyre and Sidon, now in Lebanon, were Phoenician, and the dye and colour became known as "Tyrian purple" as a result.

The process of making it was as revolting as it was laborious. The dye was extracted from the fluid of several species of murex shellfish. Living in relatively deep water, these shellfish were caught in baited traps suspended from floats. The dye was then extracted from the glands of thousands of putrefied, crushed shellfish left to bake in the sun. The resulting liquid was used to dye cloth fibres in manipulated variations of colours ranging from pink to violet. The dyeing process involves extracting the liquid while the mollusc is still alive and exposing it to sunlight for a specified period of time, during which the dye changes colour. It can take up to 12,000 molluscs to produce just one gram of dye.

The dye was greatly prized in antiquity because the colour did not easily fade, but instead became brighter with weathering and sunlight. It came in various shades, the most prized being that of black-tinted clotted blood. Because it was extremely tedious to make, Tyrian purple was expensive: the 4th-century BC historian Theopompus reported that purple for dyes "fetched its weight in silver at Colophon" in Asia Minor.

The Phoenicians gained great fame as sellers of purple and exported its manufacture to their colonies, notably Carthage, from where it spread in popularity and was adopted by the Romans as a symbol of imperial authority and status.

---

## IV. Rome: The Colour of Caesars

Another common name was "Royal purple," because it was so highly prized that only kings could afford it, and under the Romans, Tyrian purple was more valuable than gold.

Its striking colour and resistance to fading made clothing dyed with Tyrian purple highly desirable, and the ancient Romans adopted purple as a symbol of imperial authority and status. The togas of the Senators were trimmed in purple, and a completely purple toga was worn by the person occupying the powerful office of Censor. The most senior Roman magistrates wore a toga praetexta — a white toga edged in Tyrian purple. The even more sumptuous toga picta, solid Tyrian purple with gold thread edging, was worn by generals celebrating a Roman triumph.

So deeply embedded was purple in the language of Roman power that by the fourth century AD, sumptuary laws in Rome had been tightened so much that only the Roman emperor was permitted to wear Tyrian purple. As a result, "purple" became a metonym for the office itself — the phrase "donned the purple" came to mean "became emperor."

---

## V. Byzantium: Born in the Purple

The Byzantine Empire elevated purple beyond status — it became a theological and dynastic principle. By the Byzantine period, the colour had become associated with the emperors, and sumptuary laws restricted its use by anyone except the imperial household. Purple was thus seen as an imperial colour. Byzantine sumptuary laws strictly regulated purple to maintain imperial exclusivity. Laws forbade lower classes from wearing purple to prevent dilution of its sacred symbolism. Violating these laws risked harsh penalties, reinforcing purple's status as an exclusive imperial privilege.

So total was this identification that a new concept was born: *porphyrogennetos*. The Greek word "porphyrogennetos," meaning "born in the purple," was a magnificent declaration of legitimacy within the ruling class of Byzantium and a grand statement of imperial supremacy. To be "born in the purple," one had to be a child born within a particular, elegantly purple-adorned chamber — known in medieval Greek as the "Porphyra" — within the Great Palace of Constantinople.

With the fall of the Roman and then the Byzantine Empire, the European understanding of purple dyeing fell away, and by the 14th century the secrets of Tyrian purple were lost. It has only been through recent experimentation that the technique was rediscovered in 2001.

The royal class's purple monopoly finally waned after the fall of the Byzantine Empire in the 15th century, but the colour did not become more widely available until the 1850s, when the first synthetic dyes hit the market.

---

## VI. An Accidental Revolution — Mauveine, 1856

For centuries after Byzantium's fall, purple remained elusive and expensive, its ancient secrets buried. Then, in a London home laboratory, an eighteen-year-old student changed everything — by accident.

In 1856, an eighteen-year-old chemistry student named William Henry Perkin was attempting to synthesize quinine in his makeshift home laboratory when he accidentally created a vivid purple substance. Perkin was working with coal tar derivatives, specifically trying to oxidize aniline to create quinine. Coal tar, a byproduct of gas production, was considered industrial waste.

When Perkin's quinine synthesis failed, producing dark sludge, most experimenters would have discarded it. But Perkin noticed that alcohol extracted a purple substance from this sludge that stained cloth beautifully and resisted fading.
